::: {#task .lx-sec}
```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-studio-brief">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The task</p>
<ol class="lx-studio-task">
<li><b>Produce:</b> an uncertainty plan for your own study (each uncertainty, its kind, its treatment and how you will report it), and one result written as a range for a paper, a decision-maker and the public.</li>
<li><b>From:</b> a fictional study's single number, the twelve uncertainties behind it, and bands your browser computes on 2025's real hourly demand.</li>
<li><b>Done when:</b> the rubric's bar for Uncertainty: uncertainties classified; scenario or global sensitivity analysis; results as ranges.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-hint">About 30 minutes guided here, then about an hour on your own: list and sort the uncertainties of your own study, run one scenario or global sensitivity analysis on it, and write the result as a range for three readers.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-interactive lx-cards" data-learn="r06-uncertainty-properly" data-src="../assets/learn/data/r06-uncertainty-properly.json ../assets/learn/data/town_year.json ../assets/learn/data/path.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Four kinds, and one pile set apart</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Parameter:</b> a number in the model that data or judgement can bound. Sample it with the others.</li>
<li><b>Structural:</b> <span class="lx-term" data-term="structural-uncertainty">how the model is built</span>, and what it leaves out. Run another form.</li>
<li><b>Scenario:</b> an outside future with a few coherent versions. Run each, with no invented odds.</li>
<li><b>Deep:</b> <span class="lx-term" data-term="deep-uncertainty">no agreed outcomes, odds or model</span>. Show a what-if, and plan to adapt.</li>
<li><b>A choice, not an uncertainty:</b> a decision or value judgement the study informs. Compare the options; never sample them.</li>
</ul>
<!-- r06-task:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The claim</p><p class="r6-claim">“Prairie Town's peak demand will reach 515 MW in 2035.”</p>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Twelve uncertainties behind it, sorted, with reasons</summary><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Uncertainty</th><th scope="col">Pile</th><th scope="col">Why</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>How fast demand grows each year, apart from cars (0.4 to 1.6%)</td><td>Parameter</td><td>A number inside the model with a range from data: give it a range or a distribution, and sample it with the others.</td></tr>
<tr><td>How much energy one electric car draws on an average day (7 to 13 kWh)</td><td>Parameter</td><td>Another number with a defensible range, from driving surveys or meter data: sample it.</td></tr>
<tr><td>How hot the hottest afternoon of 2035 turns out to be</td><td>Parameter</td><td>Year-to-year weather is variability no study can know in advance: a parameter you sample over the range past years show.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Whether car charging adds to the town's peak hour, or mostly to later hours</td><td>Structural</td><td>The form of the model: adding peaks assumes they come in the same hour; adding hour by hour does not. Run both forms.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Using 2025's hourly pattern of demand for every year to 2035</td><td>Structural</td><td>A choice of structure (one year's pattern stands for all). Test it with another year's pattern, or state it as a limit.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Counting only cars charged at home, none charged at work</td><td>Structural</td><td>What a model leaves out is part of its structure. State it, and test a version with workplace charging.</td></tr>
<tr><td>How many electric cars the town has in 2035: 6,000, 15,000 or 30,000</td><td>Scenario</td><td>Three coherent stories about outside drivers (car prices, models, policy). Run each one; attach odds only if you can defend them.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Whether the state requires all-electric new homes after 2028</td><td>Scenario</td><td>An outside policy path with two or three clear versions: a scenario, run one by one.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Whether a large new customer, such as a factory, asks to connect, and when</td><td>Deep</td><td>No one can give odds you could defend, and its size is open. Show it as a separate what-if, and plan to adapt.</td></tr>
<tr><td>How travel changes if shared self-driving fleets arrive</td><td>Deep</td><td>Experts disagree on whether, when and how it changes charging: the outcomes themselves are unknown.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Whether the utility funds a managed-charging programme</td><td>A choice, not an uncertainty</td><td>A decision the study should inform. Run the study with and without it and compare; sampling it would hide the comparison.</td></tr>
<tr><td>How large a safety margin the utility plans above its forecast</td><td>A choice, not an uncertainty</td><td>A value judgement about risk. Show the range, and say what each margin implies; never average over margins.</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div></details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Five treatments, one for each pile</summary>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">1 · Parameter · How fast demand grows each year, apart from cars (0.4 to 1.6%)</p><ul>
<li>Use the midpoint, 1.0% a year, and report one peak. <b>Hard to defend.</b> One number hides a range the data support, and the reader cannot see how sure you are: the rubric's Developing level, “single numbers”.</li>
<li>Swing it from 0.4 to 1.6% with everything else fixed, as a tornado bar. <b>Partly.</b> A fair first screen, but one at a time it leaves most combinations unexplored, and it shows sensitivity to your chosen range, not the spread of outcomes.</li>
<li>Sample it together with the other parameters (Monte Carlo), report P10 to P90 and rank the inputs. <b>Defensible.</b> All parameters move together, so the band shows the spread the ranges imply, and the ranking says which input matters most.</li>
</ul>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">2 · Structural · Whether car charging adds to the town's peak hour, or mostly to later hours</p><ul>
<li>Widen the growth range until the band covers both model forms. <b>Hard to defend.</b> It hides a question about the model inside a parameter, and the band then answers neither.</li>
<li>Run both model forms and report the gap between them. <b>Defensible.</b> Sampling cannot reveal a structural choice; comparing forms can, and the gap tells readers how much the choice matters.</li>
<li>Use whichever form gives the higher peak, to be safe. <b>Partly.</b> Sometimes wise for a planner, but say so: readers would take a cautious bound for your best estimate.</li>
</ul>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">3 · Scenario · How many electric cars the town has in 2035: 6,000, 15,000 or 30,000</p><ul>
<li>Average the three and report the mean. <b>Hard to defend.</b> The average of three stories is a future nobody described, and it hides the spread between them.</li>
<li>Call the central one the forecast, and the other two the extremes. <b>Partly.</b> Fine if you can say why the central one is more likely; otherwise readers take a storyline for a prediction.</li>
<li>Run each one and show them side by side, with no odds attached. <b>Defensible.</b> Each storyline keeps its own band, and readers can see which assumptions drive the difference.</li>
</ul>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">4 · Deep · Whether a large new customer, such as a factory, asks to connect, and when</p><ul>
<li>Give it a 50% chance and add it to the sampled runs. <b>Hard to defend.</b> An invented 50% turns “we don't know” into a number that looks like knowledge, and it blurs the band for everyone.</li>
<li>Leave it out of the numbers, and mention it in the limits. <b>Partly.</b> Better than silence, but a 60 MW what-if is wider than much of the band: show it beside the result.</li>
<li>Show it as a separate what-if, look for a plan that holds with and without it, and name the signal that would trigger a review. <b>Defensible.</b> The approach of decision making under deep uncertainty: test plans across futures, and adapt when a signpost moves.</li>
</ul>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">5 · A choice, not an uncertainty · Whether the utility funds a managed-charging programme</p><ul>
<li>Sample it: half the runs with the programme, half without. <b>Hard to defend.</b> Mixing the two options blurs the very comparison the utility needs to make.</li>
<li>Run the study with and without the programme, and compare the two bands. <b>Defensible.</b> A choice is compared, not sampled: each option gets its own result, and the difference is what the programme is worth to the peak.</li>
<li>Assume the programme happens, since the utility has planned it. <b>Partly.</b> A plan is not a fact. Report the other case too, so readers can see what the programme changes.</li>
</ul>
</details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>The 2035 peak as bands, in numbers</summary><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Case</th><th scope="col">P10</th><th scope="col">Median</th><th scope="col">P90</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>The study's single number (peaks added, central, middle inputs)</td><td class="n" colspan="3">515 MW</td></tr>
<tr><td>Peaks added, slow uptake</td><td class="n">475</td><td class="n">500</td><td class="n">530</td></tr>
<tr><td>Peaks added, central uptake</td><td class="n">490</td><td class="n">515</td><td class="n">545</td></tr>
<tr><td>Peaks added, fast uptake</td><td class="n">510</td><td class="n">535</td><td class="n">565</td></tr>
<tr><td>Hours added, slow uptake</td><td class="n">470</td><td class="n">500</td><td class="n">525</td></tr>
<tr><td>Hours added, central uptake</td><td class="n">480</td><td class="n">505</td><td class="n">535</td></tr>
<tr><td>Hours added, fast uptake</td><td class="n">495</td><td class="n">520</td><td class="n">550</td></tr>
<tr><td>What-if: a 60 MW customer from 2030 (hours added, central)</td><td class="n" colspan="3">median 565 MW</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div><p class="lx-hint">MW, rounded to 5; 1,000 runs, seed 6; no odds across the three uptake scenarios.</p></details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>The claim rewritten for three readers (examples)</summary><dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>For a paper's results section</dt><dd>With growth (0.4–1.6% a year), a car's daily energy (7–13 kWh) and the year's weather (±4%) sampled together in 1,000 runs, the 2035 peak is 480–535 MW (P10–P90) under central car uptake and 495–550 MW under fast uptake. Demand is added hour by hour on 2025's pattern; adding peaks instead raises the central median by 10 MW.</dd>
<dt>For the utility's board, deciding what to plan for</dt><dd>Plan for up to 535 MW in 2035 under central car uptake, or 550 MW if uptake is fast: 9 in 10 model runs stay below each. A 60 MW new customer would add to either; a connection request, or car numbers on the fast path, should trigger a new forecast.</dd>
<dt>For the public, in the town's newsletter</dt><dd>In most of the futures we modelled, the town's busiest hour in 2035 needs 480 to 535 megawatts, up from 450 today; how fast demand grows matters most. If electric cars spread fast, it could reach 550. A large new factory would add more.</dd>
</dl></details>
<!-- r06-task:end -->
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you sort the cards, choose treatments, draw the bands yourself and write your own plan; your drafts stay in this browser.</p>
</div>
</div>
<p class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><span><b>Study:</b> fictional. Its ranges, car numbers, charging patterns and the 60 MW customer are illustrative.<br><b>Hourly pattern:</b> real. SPP's 2025 demand (EIA-930), scaled so the town's highest hour of 2025 is 450 MW, as in lesson 0.<br><b>Sampling:</b> 1,000 runs, seed 6; P10 and P90 by linear interpolation, as in K5; bands rounded to 5 MW.</span></p>
```

## Two answers to the same task
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r06-exemplars" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- r06-exemplars:start (written from the data file by LX.Exemplars' staticHTML in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-ex-cols">
<div class="lx-ex-ans weak"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Weak answer · Developing</p><p class="lx-ex-lines">Our model shows that Prairie Town's peak demand will reach 515 MW in 2035 [1]. We tested the sensitivity of the results and found them robust [2]. Electric cars add 18 MW to the peak [3]. Uncertainties remain, such as future policy [4].</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Falls short:</b> One number, to the megawatt, with “will”: no range and no conditions.</li><li value="2"><b>Falls short:</b> Which inputs, over what ranges? “Robust” is asserted, not shown.</li><li value="3"><b>Falls short:</b> Only if charging and the peak come in the same hour: a structural choice left unstated.</li><li value="4"><b>Falls short:</b> Not classified and not treated: which ones matter, and what was done about them?</li></ol></div>
<div class="lx-ex-ans good"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Strong answer · Proficient</p><p class="lx-ex-lines"><b>Varied:</b> growth (0.4–1.6% a year), a car's daily energy (7–13 kWh) and the year's weather (±4%), sampled together in 1,000 runs (seed 6) [1].
<b>Scenarios:</b> slow, central and fast car uptake, with no odds attached [2].
<b>Model form:</b> demand added hour by hour on 2025's pattern; adding peaks instead raises the central median by 10 MW [3].
<b>Result:</b> 480–535 MW (P10–P90) under central uptake, 495–550 MW under fast uptake [4].
<b>Drivers:</b> growth matters most (rank correlation 0.83), then weather (0.49) [5].
<b>Not in the band:</b> a 60 MW new customer, shown as a what-if [6].</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Works:</b> Parameters named, with their ranges and how they were sampled.</li><li value="2"><b>Works:</b> Scenarios kept apart, with no invented probabilities.</li><li value="3"><b>Works:</b> The structural choice stated, with what the other form changes.</li><li value="4"><b>Works:</b> Results as ranges, labelled as the central 80% of the modelled runs.</li><li value="5"><b>Works:</b> A global sensitivity ranking: which input moves the result most, with all varying together.</li><li value="6"><b>Works:</b> The deep uncertainty named and shown, not hidden in the band.</li></ol></div>
</div>
<table class="lx-facts lx-ex-diff"><thead><tr><th scope="col"></th><th scope="col">Weak answer</th><th scope="col">Strong answer</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">The number</th><td>One, with “will”</td><td>Ranges, with what they mean</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Uncertainties</th><td>“Remain”</td><td>Classified, each with a treatment</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Model form</th><td>Unstated</td><td>Stated, with its effect</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">New customer</th><td>Missing</td><td>A separate what-if</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The kinds compared</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Kind</th><th scope="col">What it is</th><th scope="col">In this study</th><th scope="col">Treatment</th><th scope="col">How to say it</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Parameter</th><td>A number in the model that data or judgement can bound.</td><td>Growth, a car's daily energy, the year's weather.</td><td>Ranges or distributions, sampled together; rank the inputs.</td><td>P10–P90 of the runs, with the ranges and their sources.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Structural</th><td>How the model is built, and what it leaves out.</td><td>Peaks added or hours added; one year's pattern; home charging only.</td><td>Run an alternative form, or benchmark against another model.</td><td>The choice made, and the gap to the alternative.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Scenario</th><td>An outside future with a few coherent versions.</td><td>Slow, central or fast car uptake; a building code.</td><td>Run each storyline separately.</td><td>Side by side, with no odds unless you can defend them.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Deep</th><td>No agreed outcomes, odds or model.</td><td>A large new customer; self-driving fleets.</td><td>Test plans across many futures; set signposts and triggers.</td><td>A what-if beside the result, and the signal that would change the advice.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">A choice (not an uncertainty)</th><td>A decision or value judgement the study informs.</td><td>Managed charging; the planning margin.</td><td>Compare the options.</td><td>One result per option.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<!-- r06-exemplars:end -->
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Which treatment?</dt><dd>Ask four questions in order. Your own choice? Compare the options. In the model's form? Run another form. A range you can defend? Sample it. A few coherent futures? Run each scenario. None of these: a deep uncertainty, shown as a what-if.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>Other ways to sort uncertainty</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><b>Variability or lack of knowledge.</b> The weather of a future year varies however much you learn (sample it); the true growth rate is fixed but unknown (more data narrows it).</li>
<li><b>Data and measurement.</b> Missing meter readings and revised statistics are uncertainties too; the cleaning log of <a href="r04-data.html">R4</a> is where they are treated.</li>
<li><b>Values.</b> A discount rate or a fairness weight is a judgement: show results across the choices, as for the utility's safety margin here.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this studio leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Variance shares (Sobol indices) and Latin hypercube sampling: <a href="m07-monte-carlo.html">M7</a> and its notebook build them. Here a rank correlation is enough to rank three inputs.</li>
<li>Asking experts for ranges in a structured way (elicitation): a topic for a statistics course.</li>
<li>Decisions that hedge across scenarios (stochastic and robust optimization): M8 (upcoming).</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check your own work against the rubric
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r06-rubric" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- r06-rubric:start (written by LX.Rubric's staticHTML, from the course rubric, and from the data file's checklist, in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts lx-rb-static"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Competence</th><th scope="col">Developing</th><th scope="col">Proficient (the bar)</th><th scope="col">Strong</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Uncertainty<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: Your plan names each uncertainty's kind and its treatment, keeps your own choices apart, and your result is a range with what it means.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Single numbers.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Uncertainties classified; scenario or global sensitivity analysis; results as ranges.</td><td data-l="Strong">Decision-relevant uncertainty identified and its value discussed.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">An uncertainty check for your own study</p>
<ul><li><b>Listed:</b> The inputs and assumptions that could change your answer, one line each.</li><li><b>Classified:</b> Each tagged parameter, structural, scenario or deep; your own choices set apart.</li><li><b>Ranges sourced:</b> Every range or distribution says where it comes from.</li><li><b>Varied together:</b> Parameters sampled together, not only one at a time; inputs ranked by influence.</li><li><b>Scenarios apart:</b> Each storyline run on its own, with no odds unless you can defend them.</li><li><b>Model form tested:</b> At least one alternative form run, or the choice stated as a limit.</li><li><b>Results as ranges:</b> Each range says what it is: P10–P90 of the modelled runs, not a guarantee.</li><li><b>Honest digits:</b> Numbers rounded to what the inputs support.</li><li><b>Deep ones named:</b> What has no odds is shown as a what-if, with the signal that would trigger a review.</li></ul>
<!-- r06-rubric:end -->
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="r6-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="tornado" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A <span class="lx-term" data-term="tornado-chart">tornado chart</span> shows how uncertain a result is.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It shows how far each input moves the result one at a time, over the ranges you chose. A review of highly cited papers found 42% did not explore the space of inputs properly (Saltelli et al., 2019, abstract).</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="mc" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A <span class="lx-term" data-term="monte-carlo">Monte Carlo</span> band gives the real-world chance of each outcome.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It is only as good as the input ranges, how they move together and the model's form. Call P10 to P90 the central 80% of the modelled runs.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="ipcc" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “When nobody knows the odds, ‘about as likely as not’ is an honest phrase.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. IPCC guidance gives that phrase a probability of 33 to 66%, and warns against using it to mean “we don't know”. Say what is unknown, and show it as a what-if.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="choice" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The options a study compares should not be sampled like uncertain inputs.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. Each option gets its own result; mixing them in one band hides the difference the decision-maker needs.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Researcher</span>From Proficient to Strong: what knowing would be worth</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>Strong asks which uncertainty would change the decision, and what resolving it would be worth: the <span class="lx-term" data-term="value-of-information">value of information</span>. A toy with two equally likely futures (illustrative payoffs):</p>
<ul>
<li>Plan A pays 12 or 2: an expected 7. Plan B pays 6 either way: an expected 6. Without a forecast, choose A.</li>
<li>With a perfect forecast you pick the better plan in each future: 12 or 6, an expected 9.</li>
<li>So a perfect forecast is worth at most 9 − 7 = 2 payoff units to someone who maximizes the expected payoff.</li>
</ul>
<p>In the capstone research project (CR, upcoming), your uncertainty plan goes into the proposal. M8 (upcoming) builds decisions that hedge before the uncertainty resolves; <a href="m07-monte-carlo.html">M7</a> builds the sampling.</p>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
